title: AI Literacy
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of AI Literacy. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: Artificial intelligence
concepts.explanation: Systems performing tasks that require reasoning, perception or decision making
concepts.example: A route planner chooses a path under constraints
concepts.trap: AI always requires neural networks

concepts.name: Machine learning
concepts.explanation: Learning patterns from data instead of explicitly coding every decision
concepts.example: A spam classifier learns from labelled emails
concepts.trap: Every decision is a manually written rule

concepts.name: Deep learning
concepts.explanation: Machine learning with multilayer neural networks
concepts.example: A convolutional network identifies defects in images
concepts.trap: Deep learning cannot process images

concepts.name: Generative AI
concepts.explanation: Models creating new content from learned distributions
concepts.example: A model drafts a summary of a document
concepts.trap: Generative models only classify existing labels

concepts.name: Large language models
concepts.explanation: Models predicting and generating sequences of tokens
concepts.example: A model completes a partially written paragraph
concepts.trap: LLMs are guaranteed factual databases

concepts.name: Tokens
concepts.explanation: Units of text processed by a language model
concepts.example: One word can be split into several subword tokens
concepts.trap: Every word is always exactly one token

concepts.name: Embeddings
concepts.explanation: Numeric vectors representing semantic features
concepts.example: Similar sentences can have nearby vectors
concepts.trap: Embeddings are encrypted original text

concepts.name: Transformers
concepts.explanation: Neural architectures using attention to relate sequence elements
concepts.example: A model relates a pronoun to an earlier noun
concepts.trap: Transformers require recurrence for every token

concepts.name: Attention
concepts.explanation: A mechanism weighting relevant parts of an input
concepts.example: A translation model focuses on relevant source words
concepts.trap: Attention assigns equal weight to every input

concepts.name: Prompt engineering
concepts.explanation: Designing instructions, context and output requirements
concepts.example: Specify audience, constraints and JSON output
concepts.trap: A longer prompt is always a better prompt

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.explanation: A plausible generated claim unsupported by evidence
concepts.example: A model invents a journal citation
concepts.trap: Fluent writing guarantees truth

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.explanation: Updating model parameters with additional training examples
concepts.example: Adapt a model to a domain-specific classification task
concepts.trap: Fine-tuning is simply adding text to a prompt

concepts.name: Inference
concepts.explanation: Using a trained model to produce predictions
concepts.example: Classify a newly received email
concepts.trap: Inference always updates model weights

concepts.name: Context window
concepts.explanation: The bounded token capacity available for a request
concepts.example: Long conversation history may need truncation
concepts.trap: A model remembers unlimited prior text

concepts.name: Vector databases
concepts.explanation: Stores supporting similarity retrieval over embeddings
concepts.example: Retrieve product documents closest to a query vector
concepts.trap: Vector retrieval is always exact keyword matching

concepts.name: RAG
concepts.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation supplies retrieved evidence to a model
concepts.example: Retrieve policy paragraphs before answering a policy question
concepts.trap: RAG requires retraining model weights

concepts.name: Agents
concepts.explanation: Systems that choose actions and tools toward a goal
concepts.example: An assistant searches documents then checks a calendar
concepts.trap: An agent needs unrestricted permissions

concepts.name: AI safety
concepts.explanation: Controls reducing harmful or unintended model behaviour
concepts.example: Require approval before a tool deletes a record
concepts.trap: Safety can be guaranteed by a single prompt

concepts.name: AI ethics
concepts.explanation: Responsible handling of fairness, transparency and accountability
concepts.example: Audit unequal error rates across groups
concepts.trap: Accuracy alone resolves all ethical concerns

concepts.name: Supervised learning
concepts.explanation: Learning from examples paired with target labels
concepts.example: Train on transactions marked fraudulent or legitimate
concepts.trap: Supervised learning has no labels

concepts.name: Unsupervised learning
concepts.explanation: Finding structure in data without target labels
concepts.example: Cluster customers by purchasing patterns
concepts.trap: Clustering needs a correct class for each sample

concepts.name: Classification
concepts.explanation: Predicting a discrete category
concepts.example: Predict whether an email is spam
concepts.trap: Classification always outputs a continuous price

concepts.name: Regression
concepts.explanation: Predicting a numeric target
concepts.example: Estimate a house price
concepts.trap: Regression only returns categories

concepts.name: Training and validation
concepts.explanation: Validation estimates performance outside training examples
concepts.example: Tune a model on validation data then evaluate on held-out tests
concepts.trap: Test data should be used repeatedly for tuning

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.explanation: Learning training-specific noise that fails to generalize
concepts.example: Training accuracy is high but validation accuracy falls
concepts.trap: Perfect training accuracy guarantees deployment quality

concepts.name: Data leakage
concepts.explanation: Training uses information unavailable at prediction time
concepts.example: A future payment status leaks into a credit-risk feature
concepts.trap: Leakage makes real-world evaluation more reliable

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.explanation: The fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive
concepts.example: Reduce false fraud alerts when review capacity is limited
concepts.trap: Precision is the fraction of all positives recovered

concepts.name: Recall
concepts.explanation: The fraction of actual positives successfully detected
concepts.example: Prioritize detecting diseases even with extra follow-up tests
concepts.trap: High recall implies there are no false positives

concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.explanation: A sampling control affecting output variability
concepts.example: Use a lower temperature for more consistent extraction
concepts.trap: Temperature guarantees factual correctness

concepts.name: Few-shot prompting
concepts.explanation: Showing examples of the desired task and format
concepts.example: Provide two labelled extraction examples in the prompt
concepts.trap: Few-shot examples permanently train the model

concepts.name: System instructions
concepts.explanation: Application-level instructions for model behaviour
concepts.example: Set a tutoring policy before candidate input
concepts.trap: User text should be allowed to override all safety rules

concepts.name: Prompt injection
concepts.explanation: Untrusted content tries to override trusted instructions
concepts.example: A retrieved page says to ignore the developer instructions
concepts.trap: Retrieved documents are always trusted instructions

concepts.name: Retrieval loaders
concepts.explanation: Components reading source data into document records
concepts.example: Load a PDF with page metadata
concepts.trap: A loader automatically verifies every source claim

concepts.name: Chunking
concepts.explanation: Splitting documents into retrieval units
concepts.example: Split a handbook into overlapping sections
concepts.trap: One entire corpus should always be a single chunk

concepts.name: Recursive splitting
concepts.explanation: Splitting progressively by section, paragraph and smaller boundaries
concepts.example: Try paragraph breaks before splitting individual sentences
concepts.trap: Recursive splitting is identical to random splitting

concepts.name: Semantic splitting
concepts.explanation: Grouping text based on meaning changes
concepts.example: Start a new chunk when the discussion changes topic
concepts.trap: Semantic splitting always uses a fixed character count

concepts.name: Chunk overlap
concepts.explanation: Repeating some boundary content to preserve context
concepts.example: Repeat a preceding sentence in the next chunk
concepts.trap: Overlap has no storage or token cost

concepts.name: Cosine similarity
concepts.explanation: Measures alignment of two vectors independent of magnitude
concepts.example: Compare normalized query and document directions
concepts.trap: A higher cosine score proves a source is factually true

concepts.name: Top-K retrieval
concepts.explanation: Returning a limited number of nearest candidates
concepts.example: Fetch five relevant chunks for an answer
concepts.trap: Larger K always improves quality without cost

concepts.name: Retriever
concepts.explanation: Selects evidence for a query from an indexed corpus
concepts.example: Apply a policy-year filter before vector search
concepts.trap: The retriever must write the final natural-language answer

concepts.name: Prompt construction
concepts.explanation: Combining instructions, query and clearly delimited evidence
concepts.example: Tell the model to cite supplied passages and admit missing evidence
concepts.trap: Retrieved content should be treated as new system instructions

concepts.name: Reranking
concepts.explanation: Reordering initial candidates using a more precise relevance model
concepts.example: Score query-document pairs after broad vector retrieval
concepts.trap: Reranking must happen before any candidates are retrieved

concepts.name: Metadata filtering
concepts.explanation: Restricting search using structured document attributes
concepts.example: Only retrieve records accessible to the current department
concepts.trap: Similarity search automatically enforces access control

concepts.name: Hybrid search
concepts.explanation: Combining lexical and semantic retrieval
concepts.example: Use keywords for an exact product code and vectors for intent
concepts.trap: Hybrid search excludes keyword search

concepts.name: RAG evaluation
concepts.explanation: Assessing retrieval relevance and grounded answer quality
concepts.example: Measure retrieval recall and answer faithfulness separately
concepts.trap: Only grammar quality matters for a RAG system

concepts.name: Grounded generation
concepts.explanation: Supporting generated claims with supplied evidence
concepts.example: Answer with a cited policy section or abstain
concepts.trap: RAG completely eliminates hallucinations

concepts.name: Embedding consistency
concepts.explanation: Index and query vectors must use compatible embedding spaces
concepts.example: Re-embed documents when switching embedding models
concepts.trap: Vectors from unrelated embedding models are interchangeable

concepts.name: Index freshness
concepts.explanation: An index needs updates when source documents change
concepts.example: Refresh a handbook index after a policy revision
concepts.trap: RAG indexes stay current without an update process

concepts.name: Retrieval access control
concepts.explanation: Authorization must constrain evidence retrieval
concepts.example: Filter restricted records before constructing model context
concepts.trap: Hiding a final citation is sufficient protection

concepts.name: Tool calling
concepts.explanation: Models request structured actions which the application validates
concepts.example: Validate arguments before invoking a database lookup
concepts.trap: A model tool call is automatically safe to execute

title: DBMS
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of DBMS. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: DBMS vs RDBMS
concepts.explanation: An RDBMS organizes relations with relational constraints
concepts.example: Represent customers and orders in linked tables
concepts.trap: Every DBMS must store only relational tables

concepts.name: Primary key
concepts.explanation: Uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null
concepts.example: A customer_id identifies a customer record
concepts.trap: A primary key may contain duplicate values

concepts.name: Foreign key
concepts.explanation: References a candidate key to maintain referential integrity
concepts.example: An order customer_id references a customer
concepts.trap: A foreign key must be unique in the child table

concepts.name: Candidate key
concepts.explanation: A minimal set of attributes uniquely identifying a row
concepts.example: Both employee_id and a unique email can be candidates
concepts.trap: A candidate key may include redundant attributes

concepts.name: First normal form
concepts.explanation: Each attribute holds an atomic value relative to its domain
concepts.example: Store each phone number in a separate related row
concepts.trap: Comma-separated repeating phone fields always satisfy 1NF

concepts.name: Second normal form
concepts.explanation: 1NF with no partial dependency on a candidate key
concepts.example: Move a product name out of a composite order-item key table
concepts.trap: 2NF allows dependency on only part of a composite key

concepts.name: Third normal form
concepts.explanation: For every dependency X to A, X is a superkey or A is prime
concepts.example: Separate department details from employee details
concepts.trap: 3NF always permits transitive dependencies on non-key attributes

concepts.name: BCNF
concepts.explanation: Every determinant in a nontrivial dependency is a superkey
concepts.example: Decompose a relation whose non-key tutor determines a subject
concepts.trap: BCNF is weaker than third normal form

concepts.name: Atomicity
concepts.explanation: A transaction completes entirely or rolls back
concepts.example: Both debit and credit succeed in a transfer
concepts.trap: Atomicity permits a partially committed transfer

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.explanation: A transaction preserves defined integrity constraints
concepts.example: A balance check prevents invalid negative balances
concepts.trap: Consistency means all replicas are instantly identical

concepts.name: Isolation
concepts.explanation: Concurrent transactions follow an isolation contract
concepts.example: A serializable schedule behaves like a serial order
concepts.trap: Isolation means no transactions can ever run concurrently

concepts.name: Durability
concepts.explanation: Committed changes survive supported failures
concepts.example: Recover committed orders after a restart
concepts.trap: Committed data exists only in volatile memory

concepts.name: Clustered index
concepts.explanation: Defines row storage ordering or clustering in an engine-specific way
concepts.example: Range scans can benefit from clustered key locality
concepts.trap: A table can have unlimited independent physical row orders

concepts.name: Non-clustered index
concepts.explanation: Separate search structure pointing to underlying rows
concepts.example: Look up an employee by an indexed email
concepts.trap: An index makes every write operation cheaper

concepts.name: Joins
concepts.explanation: Combine related rows based on a condition
concepts.example: Join invoices to customers using customer_id
concepts.trap: A join always removes unmatched rows

concepts.name: Views
concepts.explanation: Named queries exposing a derived representation
concepts.example: Expose selected columns to reporting users
concepts.trap: Every ordinary view stores a separate physical copy

concepts.name: Stored procedures
concepts.explanation: Named server-side routines containing database logic
concepts.example: A routine applies a sequence of validated updates
concepts.trap: Stored procedures inherently prevent all injection

concepts.name: Triggers
concepts.explanation: Routines invoked by configured database events
concepts.example: Write an audit row after an update
concepts.trap: Triggers execute only when manually called by name

concepts.name: Deadlocks
concepts.explanation: Transactions form a cycle of mutually waiting locks
concepts.example: Transaction A holds X while B holds Y and both request the other
concepts.trap: A deadlock is the same as a single long query

concepts.name: Isolation levels
concepts.explanation: Trade-offs controlling allowed concurrent-read anomalies
concepts.example: Read committed avoids dirty reads but may allow nonrepeatable reads
concepts.trap: Read committed prevents every phantom under every engine

concepts.name: Transactions and concurrency
concepts.explanation: A transaction groups work while concurrency coordinates interleaved operations
concepts.example: Transfer funds with a consistent lock ordering and rollback on failure
concepts.trap: Every transaction must execute entirely alone

title: SQL
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of SQL. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: SELECT
concepts.explanation: Projects expressions or columns from matching rows
concepts.example: SELECT name FROM employees
concepts.trap: SELECT always changes stored rows

concepts.name: WHERE
concepts.explanation: Filters individual rows before grouping
concepts.example: WHERE salary > 50000
concepts.trap: WHERE filters aggregate groups after GROUP BY

concepts.name: GROUP BY
concepts.explanation: Forms groups sharing grouping expressions
concepts.example: GROUP BY department
concepts.trap: GROUP BY guarantees sorted output

concepts.name: HAVING
concepts.explanation: Filters aggregate groups
concepts.example: HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
concepts.trap: HAVING must always execute before WHERE

concepts.name: ORDER BY
concepts.explanation: Defines result ordering
concepts.example: ORDER BY salary DESC, id ASC
concepts.trap: Rows have guaranteed order without ORDER BY

concepts.name: INNER JOIN
concepts.explanation: Returns rows matching the join condition on both sides
concepts.example: Join orders to existing customers
concepts.trap: An inner join always preserves every left row

concepts.name: LEFT JOIN
concepts.explanation: Preserves left rows and null-extends unmatched right columns
concepts.example: List all customers even those without orders
concepts.trap: Filtering right columns in WHERE always preserves unmatched left rows

concepts.name: RIGHT JOIN
concepts.explanation: Preserves right rows and null-extends unmatched left columns
concepts.example: Keep all right-table departments
concepts.trap: RIGHT JOIN is identical to INNER JOIN for unmatched rows

concepts.name: SELF JOIN
concepts.explanation: Joins two aliases of the same relation
concepts.example: Link employees to managers in the employees table
concepts.trap: A self join requires two different physical tables

concepts.name: Subqueries
concepts.explanation: Queries nested within another SQL expression
concepts.example: Filter salaries above SELECT AVG(salary)
concepts.trap: A scalar subquery may return arbitrary multiple rows

concepts.name: CTE
concepts.explanation: A named query expression scoped to a statement
concepts.example: WITH totals AS (...) SELECT * FROM totals
concepts.trap: Every CTE is automatically a permanent table

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.explanation: Calculate across related rows without collapsing each output row
concepts.example: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)
concepts.trap: Window functions always reduce each partition to one row

concepts.name: COUNT
concepts.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) excludes nulls
concepts.example: COUNT(email) ignores missing emails
concepts.trap: COUNT(column) always includes null values

concepts.name: SUM and AVG
concepts.explanation: Aggregate numeric values while ignoring null inputs
concepts.example: AVG(score) ignores absent scores
concepts.trap: AVG treats every null as zero

concepts.name: MAX and MIN
concepts.explanation: Return extreme non-null values
concepts.example: MAX(salary) returns the largest known salary
concepts.trap: MAX always returns the row containing all associated columns

concepts.name: DISTINCT
concepts.explanation: Removes duplicate result tuples
concepts.example: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers
concepts.trap: DISTINCT applies only to the first selected column

concepts.name: NULL comparisons
concepts.explanation: Use IS NULL instead of equality to detect nulls
concepts.example: WHERE manager_id IS NULL
concepts.trap: NULL = NULL evaluates to true in ordinary SQL

concepts.name: UNION
concepts.explanation: Combines result sets removing duplicates unless UNION ALL is used
concepts.example: Combine active and archived customer IDs
concepts.trap: UNION ALL removes duplicates

concepts.name: Ranking functions
concepts.explanation: ROW_NUMBER assigns distinct positions while RANK leaves gaps on ties
concepts.example: Scores 90,90,80 receive RANK values 1,1,3
concepts.trap: RANK and DENSE_RANK always produce identical ranks

concepts.name: Index-aware predicates
concepts.explanation: Search-friendly predicates can permit useful index access
concepts.example: A direct timestamp range can use a timestamp index
concepts.trap: Wrapping an indexed column in a function always preserves index seeks

concepts.name: Aggregate functions
concepts.explanation: COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX and AVG summarize selected values
concepts.example: SELECT team,SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY team HAVING SUM(amount)>100
concepts.trap: HAVING and WHERE always filter at the same stage

title: OOP
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of OOP. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.explanation: A class defines structure and behaviour while an object is an instance
concepts.example: Two account objects share a class but have separate balances
concepts.trap: All instances always share every field value

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.explanation: Controls access to state through defined interfaces
concepts.example: Validate balance changes in a deposit method
concepts.trap: Public access to every mutable field guarantees encapsulation

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.explanation: A subtype derives behaviour from a parent type
concepts.example: A specialized account inherits account operations
concepts.trap: Inheritance always makes composition unnecessary

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.explanation: A common interface supports different implementations
concepts.example: Call draw on different shape objects
concepts.trap: Polymorphism requires all methods to have identical bodies

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.explanation: Exposes relevant operations while hiding implementation details
concepts.example: A payment interface hides provider-specific request logic
concepts.trap: Abstraction means every detail must be publicly visible

concepts.name: Overriding
concepts.explanation: A subtype supplies an implementation of an inherited method
concepts.example: A savings account overrides interest calculation
concepts.trap: Overriding is adding an unrelated method name

concepts.name: Overloading
concepts.explanation: Methods share a name but have distinguishable signatures in supporting languages
concepts.example: Java methods accept either an int or a String
concepts.trap: Changing only the return type permits Java overloads

concepts.name: Constructors
concepts.explanation: Initialize a new instance according to language rules
concepts.example: Set required fields when creating an account
concepts.trap: A constructor is an ordinary Java method with a return type

concepts.name: Interfaces
concepts.explanation: Specify a contract implemented by compatible types
concepts.example: Different storage providers implement a save contract
concepts.trap: An interface forces every implementation to use the same algorithm

concepts.name: Abstract classes
concepts.explanation: Can define shared implementation and abstract operations
concepts.example: A base report defines common formatting and abstract data loading
concepts.trap: An abstract class is directly instantiable in Java

concepts.name: Static members
concepts.explanation: Belong to a class rather than a particular instance
concepts.example: A shared factory method creates instances
concepts.trap: A static Java method can directly use this

concepts.name: Composition
concepts.explanation: Builds behaviour by containing or delegating to components
concepts.example: A car has an engine rather than being an engine
concepts.trap: Has-a relationships always require inheritance

concepts.name: Liskov substitution
concepts.explanation: Subtypes should preserve behavioural expectations of their base type
concepts.example: A subtype accepts calls valid for the base contract
concepts.trap: A subtype may freely strengthen every precondition

title: Operating Systems
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of OS. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: Processes and threads
concepts.explanation: Threads share a process address space while processes have isolated address spaces
concepts.example: Two worker threads access the same heap
concepts.trap: Each thread always owns a separate process address space

concepts.name: FCFS scheduling
concepts.explanation: Runs ready work in arrival order without preemption in its basic form
concepts.example: A short job waits behind a long arriving job
concepts.trap: FCFS always minimizes average waiting time

concepts.name: SJF scheduling
concepts.explanation: Chooses the shortest estimated next CPU burst
concepts.example: A short ready job runs before a longer one
concepts.trap: SJF cannot starve long jobs

concepts.name: Round Robin
concepts.explanation: Cycles ready processes with a time quantum
concepts.example: A process is preempted when its quantum expires
concepts.trap: A smaller quantum has no context-switch overhead

concepts.name: Priority scheduling
concepts.explanation: Chooses work by priority and can use aging to reduce starvation
concepts.example: Raise priority gradually for a long-waiting job
concepts.trap: Priority scheduling inherently prevents starvation

concepts.name: Context switching
concepts.explanation: Saving and restoring execution state between scheduled tasks
concepts.example: The scheduler switches register state to another thread
concepts.trap: Context switching always performs useful application computation

concepts.name: Deadlock conditions
concepts.explanation: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait are jointly necessary
concepts.example: A lock acquisition cycle can trap waiting threads
concepts.trap: Removing a necessary condition cannot prevent deadlock

concepts.name: Mutex and semaphore
concepts.explanation: A mutex protects ownership-based exclusion; a semaphore counts permits
concepts.example: A semaphore limits simultaneous workers to three
concepts.trap: A counting semaphore can only ever have value one

concepts.name: Producer consumer
concepts.explanation: Coordinates bounded-buffer production and consumption
concepts.example: Use empty/full counts with exclusion around buffer updates
concepts.trap: Only a mutex guarantees consumers never read an empty buffer

concepts.name: Readers writers
concepts.explanation: Allows concurrent readers while synchronizing writes
concepts.example: Protect a cache with a reader-writer policy
concepts.trap: All readers must always exclude one another

concepts.name: Paging
concepts.explanation: Maps fixed-size virtual pages to physical frames
concepts.example: A page table maps virtual addresses
concepts.trap: Paging requires every process to occupy contiguous physical memory

concepts.name: Virtual memory
concepts.explanation: Provides virtual address spaces backed by memory and possibly storage
concepts.example: A page fault loads a nonresident page
concepts.trap: A page fault always means an invalid address

concepts.name: Thrashing and replacement
concepts.explanation: Excessive page faults can dominate execution when working sets do not fit
concepts.example: Reduce multiprogramming when paging activity overwhelms useful work
concepts.trap: More active processes always reduce thrashing

concepts.name: Segmentation
concepts.explanation: Divides address spaces into variable-size logical regions
concepts.example: Separate code, stack and data segments
concepts.trap: Segmentation has only fixed-size frames

concepts.name: FIFO and LRU replacement
concepts.explanation: FIFO evicts by arrival; LRU evicts by recent use
concepts.example: Track last access to estimate recency
concepts.trap: FIFO and LRU always evict the same page

concepts.name: Dining philosophers
concepts.explanation: A synchronization model exposing circular-wait and resource-allocation problems
concepts.example: Acquire forks in a global order to break a cycle
concepts.trap: Each philosopher acquiring one fork guarantees progress

title: Computer Networks
summary: Build assessment-ready understanding of CN. Study the concept, trace the example, and explain the trap before practicing.

concepts.name: OSI layers
concepts.explanation: A seven-layer reference model separates networking responsibilities
concepts.example: Routing is associated with the network layer
concepts.trap: Routing is exclusively a presentation-layer function

concepts.name: TCP/IP
concepts.explanation: An Internet protocol suite spanning link, internet, transport and application functions
concepts.example: IP routes packets while TCP provides a reliable stream
concepts.trap: TCP/IP and OSI require identical layer counts

concepts.name: TCP vs UDP
concepts.explanation: TCP provides ordered reliable streams; UDP provides datagrams without that guarantee
concepts.example: Use UDP where low-latency application-managed delivery is preferred
concepts.trap: UDP guarantees retransmission and ordered delivery

concepts.name: HTTP and HTTPS
concepts.explanation: HTTPS carries HTTP over authenticated encrypted TLS connections
concepts.example: A browser verifies a server certificate during TLS
concepts.trap: HTTPS proves every webpage statement is trustworthy

concepts.name: DNS
concepts.explanation: Resolves names and other records using distributed DNS infrastructure
concepts.example: Resolve a hostname to an address before connecting
concepts.trap: DNS assigns a device its network lease

concepts.name: DHCP
concepts.explanation: Automatically supplies network configuration leases
concepts.example: A new laptop receives an IP address and gateway
concepts.trap: DHCP is the same as resolving a hostname

concepts.name: ARP
concepts.explanation: Resolves IPv4 neighbours to link-layer addresses on a local network
concepts.example: Find the MAC address for the local next hop
concepts.trap: ARP directly resolves an arbitrary remote host across the Internet

concepts.name: Subnetting
concepts.explanation: An address prefix identifies a network portion
concepts.example: A conventional IPv4 /24 subnet has 256 addresses
concepts.trap: Every /24 has 256 usable host addresses in conventional allocation

concepts.name: Routers and switches
concepts.explanation: Routers forward between networks while switches typically forward local Ethernet frames
concepts.example: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings
concepts.trap: An Ethernet hub learns destination MAC routes

concepts.name: TCP handshake and ports
concepts.explanation: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK establish a TCP connection; ports identify endpoints
concepts.example: HTTPS commonly uses TCP port 443
concepts.trap: TCP establishes a connection using only one SYN packet

title: RAG
summary: Understand RAG through mechanisms, examples, and assessment traps.

concepts.name: Retrieval loaders
concepts.explanation: Components reading source data into document records
concepts.example: Load a PDF with page metadata
concepts.trap: A loader automatically verifies every source claim

concepts.name: Chunking
concepts.explanation: Splitting documents into retrieval units
concepts.example: Split a handbook into overlapping sections
concepts.trap: One entire corpus should always be a single chunk

concepts.name: Recursive splitting
concepts.explanation: Splitting progressively by section, paragraph and smaller boundaries
concepts.example: Try paragraph breaks before splitting individual sentences
concepts.trap: Recursive splitting is identical to random splitting

concepts.name: Semantic splitting
concepts.explanation: Grouping text based on meaning changes
concepts.example: Start a new chunk when the discussion changes topic
concepts.trap: Semantic splitting always uses a fixed character count

concepts.name: Chunk overlap
concepts.explanation: Repeating some boundary content to preserve context
concepts.example: Repeat a preceding sentence in the next chunk
concepts.trap: Overlap has no storage or token cost

concepts.name: Cosine similarity
concepts.explanation: Measures alignment of two vectors independent of magnitude
concepts.example: Compare normalized query and document directions
concepts.trap: A higher cosine score proves a source is factually true

concepts.name: Top-K retrieval
concepts.explanation: Returning a limited number of nearest candidates
concepts.example: Fetch five relevant chunks for an answer
concepts.trap: Larger K always improves quality without cost

concepts.name: Retriever
concepts.explanation: Selects evidence for a query from an indexed corpus
concepts.example: Apply a policy-year filter before vector search
concepts.trap: The retriever must write the final natural-language answer

concepts.name: Prompt construction
concepts.explanation: Combining instructions, query and clearly delimited evidence
concepts.example: Tell the model to cite supplied passages and admit missing evidence
concepts.trap: Retrieved content should be treated as new system instructions

concepts.name: Reranking
concepts.explanation: Reordering initial candidates using a more precise relevance model
concepts.example: Score query-document pairs after broad vector retrieval
concepts.trap: Reranking must happen before any candidates are retrieved

concepts.name: Metadata filtering
concepts.explanation: Restricting search using structured document attributes
concepts.example: Only retrieve records accessible to the current department
concepts.trap: Similarity search automatically enforces access control

concepts.name: Hybrid search
concepts.explanation: Combining lexical and semantic retrieval
concepts.example: Use keywords for an exact product code and vectors for intent
concepts.trap: Hybrid search excludes keyword search

concepts.name: RAG evaluation
concepts.explanation: Assessing retrieval relevance and grounded answer quality
concepts.example: Measure retrieval recall and answer faithfulness separately
concepts.trap: Only grammar quality matters for a RAG system

concepts.name: Grounded generation
concepts.explanation: Supporting generated claims with supplied evidence
concepts.example: Answer with a cited policy section or abstain
concepts.trap: RAG completely eliminates hallucinations

concepts.name: Embedding consistency
concepts.explanation: Index and query vectors must use compatible embedding spaces
concepts.example: Re-embed documents when switching embedding models
concepts.trap: Vectors from unrelated embedding models are interchangeable

concepts.name: Index freshness
concepts.explanation: An index needs updates when source documents change
concepts.example: Refresh a handbook index after a policy revision
concepts.trap: RAG indexes stay current without an update process

concepts.name: Retrieval access control
concepts.explanation: Authorization must constrain evidence retrieval
concepts.example: Filter restricted records before constructing model context
concepts.trap: Hiding a final citation is sufficient protection

concepts.name: Tool calling
concepts.explanation: Models request structured actions which the application validates
concepts.example: Validate arguments before invoking a database lookup
concepts.trap: A model tool call is automatically safe to execute

title: Generative AI
summary: Understand Generative AI through mechanisms, examples, and assessment traps.

concepts.name: Generative AI
concepts.explanation: Models creating new content from learned distributions
concepts.example: A model drafts a summary of a document
concepts.trap: Generative models only classify existing labels

concepts.name: Large language models
concepts.explanation: Models predicting and generating sequences of tokens
concepts.example: A model completes a partially written paragraph
concepts.trap: LLMs are guaranteed factual databases

concepts.name: Tokens
concepts.explanation: Units of text processed by a language model
concepts.example: One word can be split into several subword tokens
concepts.trap: Every word is always exactly one token

concepts.name: Embeddings
concepts.explanation: Numeric vectors representing semantic features
concepts.example: Similar sentences can have nearby vectors
concepts.trap: Embeddings are encrypted original text

concepts.name: Transformers
concepts.explanation: Neural architectures using attention to relate sequence elements
concepts.example: A model relates a pronoun to an earlier noun
concepts.trap: Transformers require recurrence for every token

concepts.name: Attention
concepts.explanation: A mechanism weighting relevant parts of an input
concepts.example: A translation model focuses on relevant source words
concepts.trap: Attention assigns equal weight to every input

concepts.name: Prompt engineering
concepts.explanation: Designing instructions, context and output requirements
concepts.example: Specify audience, constraints and JSON output
concepts.trap: A longer prompt is always a better prompt

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.explanation: A plausible generated claim unsupported by evidence
concepts.example: A model invents a journal citation
concepts.trap: Fluent writing guarantees truth

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.explanation: Updating model parameters with additional training examples
concepts.example: Adapt a model to a domain-specific classification task
concepts.trap: Fine-tuning is simply adding text to a prompt

concepts.name: Inference
concepts.explanation: Using a trained model to produce predictions
concepts.example: Classify a newly received email
concepts.trap: Inference always updates model weights

concepts.name: Context window
concepts.explanation: The bounded token capacity available for a request
concepts.example: Long conversation history may need truncation
concepts.trap: A model remembers unlimited prior text

concepts.name: Vector databases
concepts.explanation: Stores supporting similarity retrieval over embeddings
concepts.example: Retrieve product documents closest to a query vector
concepts.trap: Vector retrieval is always exact keyword matching

concepts.name: RAG
concepts.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation supplies retrieved evidence to a model
concepts.example: Retrieve policy paragraphs before answering a policy question
concepts.trap: RAG requires retraining model weights

concepts.name: Agents
concepts.explanation: Systems that choose actions and tools toward a goal
concepts.example: An assistant searches documents then checks a calendar
concepts.trap: An agent needs unrestricted permissions

concepts.name: AI safety
concepts.explanation: Controls reducing harmful or unintended model behaviour
concepts.example: Require approval before a tool deletes a record
concepts.trap: Safety can be guaranteed by a single prompt

concepts.name: AI ethics
concepts.explanation: Responsible handling of fairness, transparency and accountability
concepts.example: Audit unequal error rates across groups
concepts.trap: Accuracy alone resolves all ethical concerns

title: Technical Fundamentals
summary: Understand Technical Fundamentals through mechanisms, examples, and assessment traps.

concepts.name: DBMS vs RDBMS
concepts.explanation: An RDBMS organizes relations with relational constraints
concepts.example: Represent customers and orders in linked tables
concepts.trap: Every DBMS must store only relational tables

concepts.name: Primary key
concepts.explanation: Uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null
concepts.example: A customer_id identifies a customer record
concepts.trap: A primary key may contain duplicate values

concepts.name: Foreign key
concepts.explanation: References a candidate key to maintain referential integrity
concepts.example: An order customer_id references a customer
concepts.trap: A foreign key must be unique in the child table

concepts.name: Candidate key
concepts.explanation: A minimal set of attributes uniquely identifying a row
concepts.example: Both employee_id and a unique email can be candidates
concepts.trap: A candidate key may include redundant attributes

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.explanation: A class defines structure and behaviour while an object is an instance
concepts.example: Two account objects share a class but have separate balances
concepts.trap: All instances always share every field value

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.explanation: Controls access to state through defined interfaces
concepts.example: Validate balance changes in a deposit method
concepts.trap: Public access to every mutable field guarantees encapsulation

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.explanation: A subtype derives behaviour from a parent type
concepts.example: A specialized account inherits account operations
concepts.trap: Inheritance always makes composition unnecessary

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.explanation: A common interface supports different implementations
concepts.example: Call draw on different shape objects
concepts.trap: Polymorphism requires all methods to have identical bodies

concepts.name: Processes and threads
concepts.explanation: Threads share a process address space while processes have isolated address spaces
concepts.example: Two worker threads access the same heap
concepts.trap: Each thread always owns a separate process address space

concepts.name: FCFS scheduling

concepts.example: A short job waits behind a long arriving job
concepts.trap: FCFS always minimizes average waiting time

concepts.name: SJF scheduling
concepts.explanation: Chooses the shortest estimated next CPU burst
concepts.example: A short ready job runs before a longer one
concepts.trap: SJF cannot starve long jobs

concepts.name: OSI layers

concepts.example: Routing is associated with the network layer
concepts.trap: Routing is exclusively a presentation-layer function

concepts.name: TCP/IP
concepts.explanation: An Internet protocol suite spanning link, internet, transport and application functions
concepts.example: IP routes packets while TCP provides a reliable stream
concepts.trap: TCP/IP and OSI require identical layer counts

concepts.explanation: TCP provides ordered reliable streams; UDP provides datagrams without that guarantee
concepts.example: Use UDP where low-latency application-managed delivery is preferred
concepts.trap: UDP guarantees retransmission and ordered delivery

title: DSA
summary: Understand DSA through mechanisms, examples, and assessment traps.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.explanation: Indexed contiguous logical sequences provide O(1) access
concepts.example: Scan once to find a maximum
concepts.trap: Repeated insertion at the start is constant time

concepts.name: Hashing
concepts.explanation: Maps provide expected O(1) lookup with collision handling
concepts.example: Store complements for a two-sum search
concepts.trap: Hash maps guarantee O(1) worst-case lookup

concepts.name: Two pointers
concepts.explanation: Move two indices according to an invariant
concepts.example: Compare sorted values at opposite ends
concepts.trap: Pointers may move without preserving the invariant

concepts.name: Sliding window
concepts.explanation: Maintain state over a moving contiguous range
concepts.example: Update a fixed-window sum by one addition and subtraction
concepts.trap: Negative values never affect variable-window reasoning

concepts.name: Binary search
concepts.explanation: Halve a monotone search space
concepts.example: Find the first true predicate in a sorted domain
concepts.trap: Binary search works on every unsorted input

concepts.name: Stacks and queues
concepts.explanation: Stacks are LIFO and queues are FIFO
concepts.example: Use a stack to match brackets
concepts.trap: A queue removes the newest element first

concepts.name: Trees and graphs
concepts.explanation: Model hierarchical and arbitrary relationships
concepts.example: Use BFS for unweighted shortest paths
concepts.trap: DFS always finds the shortest unweighted path

concepts.name: Complexity
concepts.explanation: Describe resource growth relative to input size
concepts.example: A single scan with a set takes expected O(n) time and O(n) space
concepts.trap: O(n) time means exactly n milliseconds
